name: Sustainable development
summary: Sustainable development is the UN-centred policy doctrine, set out in the 1987 Brundtland report, the 1992 Rio Declaration and Agenda 21 and the 2030 Agenda, that growth should meet present needs without compromising future generations. It joins economic growth, social inclusion and environmental protection, gives priority to the world's poor, and relies on international cooperation, open trade and aid, while leaving most questions of domestic government unaddressed.
scope: The mainstream doctrine as stated in four UN texts (Our Common Future 1987, the Rio Declaration 1992, Agenda 21 1992, the 2030 Agenda 2015) and the scholarship on the concept (Purvis et al. on the three pillars; Beckerman on the weak and strong versions). It excludes degrowth, deep ecology and 'strong sustainability' readings, which have their own literature and which these texts do not state.

missingStatements.text: Rich countries should take the lead in changing their patterns of consumption and production, because they bear more responsibility for global environmental damage than poor countries.
missingStatements.rationale: Rio Principle 7 and Agenda 21 chapter 4 place the leading duty on developed countries, the core of common but differentiated responsibilities.

quotes.text: In view of the different contributions to global environmental degradation, States have common but differentiated responsibilities.
Developed countries should take the lead in achieving sustainable consumption patterns;

missingStatements.text: Environmental protection and economic development should be pursued together, not traded against each other.
missingStatements.rationale: Both the Brundtland report and the Rio Declaration treat environment and development as one task.

quotes.text: Environment and development are not separate challenges; they are inexorably linked.
environmental protection shall constitute an integral part of the development process and cannot be considered in isolation from it.

notes: Themes searched in the four texts: economy and trade, taxes and finance, work and unions, gender, indigenous peoples, migration, health, energy and nuclear, population, climate, arms and peace, governance and participation, culture, technology. The texts say little on regime type, courts, religion, family, drugs, policing, monetary policy or ideology of the state, so those stay null. Answers mostly rest on the UN documents as primary statements of the doctrine. Beckerman's critique is cited for scope only.
